The Cümbüş is a Turkish chordophone, originally made as a cheaper substitute for the oud. It looks rather like a banjo, with an aluminium resonating bowl and a skin soundboard; the standard model is fretless, and there are fretted versions such as guitar, mandolin and ukulele, the neck angle can be set with a screw, and the wooden-bowl version has a softer timbre. It is plucked, and the set-up can be changed by swapping necks and strings; it is used in Turkish folk music, at weddings and parties, and is taken up by professional Roma musicians; it also appears in the music of Armenian, Jewish, Kurdish and Roma communities, and in modern Turkish rock and electronic music.

Modern Turkish rock and techno use it too. In Western popular music, David Lindley and Ry Cooder played it on the soundtrack of the film Paris, Texas; David Gilmour used it on the tracks “Then I Close My Eyes” and “Castellorizon” from his solo album; and Smokey Hormel has played it on Tom Waits's albums.

坎布什琴為土耳其弦鳴樂器，1930年由Zeynel Abidin Cümbüş開: The Cümbüş is a Turkish chordophone developed in 1930 by Zeynel Abidin Cümbüş, modelled on the oud but made to be heard easily in an ensemble. The name comes from the Turkish word for “revelry”. After the surname law of 1934 he took the instrument's name as his surname. After the Turkish War of Independence he turned to instrument making and showed Atatürk an instrument that was cheap, easy to carry, hard-wearing, and able to play both Eastern alaturka and Western alafranga music by changing the neck. It later became a folk instrument of the poor and of Armenian, Jewish, Kurdish and Roma communities, and classical musicians rejected it; its use declined in the 1960s, and only professional Roma players kept it for the volume it gives at weddings and parties. After the folk music revival of the mid-1990s it entered Turkish rock and electronic music again.
坎布什琴音色明亮而富有穿透力，具有獨特的金屬質感和清脆的音響特徵。其皮膚音板與旋: The Cümbüş has a bright, penetrating timbre with a distinct metallic quality and a crisp ring. The combination of a skin soundboard and a spun aluminium resonating bowl gives the instrument a clear tone that can be heard easily in a band. The range lies mainly in the upper middle register, and the notes are crisp and springy. Because of the skin soundboard, its resonance has both the warmth of a folk instrument and the projection of a modern one. Compared with the weight and softness of the oud, the Cümbüş is brighter and more penetrating; compared with the American five-string banjo, its timbre has more of an eastern character, with the particular flavour of Turkish folk music, a sound that is both traditional and modern.
